summaries.example: Imagine a row of toy blocks. Each block is held up by another block, but there is no block at the bottom. You can explain why one block stays up by pointing to the next block, and then explain that block by pointing to another. Some people think the whole tower still needs a bottom support. Others think each individual connection has been explained, even though the whole tower has no single starting support.
summaries.summary: An infinite regress is an endless chain in which each part leads to another part. Philosophers use infinite regress arguments to test theories. Sometimes the regress shows a clear problem, such as a contradiction. Sometimes it only shows that a theory includes infinitely many things, which may or may not be bad. A chain of natural numbers can be harmless, while an endless chain of causes or supports may seem to leave something unexplained. Philosophers disagree about what a good explanation must do. Some seek a foundation, some accept a connected whole, and some accept an infinite chain. The important lesson is that we should ask what the regress is meant to explain and whether every step depends on the next one.
key_ideas: An endless series is not automatically a mistake. We must ask what kind of series it is.
A regress may reveal a contradiction, such as rules that cannot all be true together.
An endless supply of natural numbers seems less troubling than an endless chain of past events, because we may know different things about these subjects.
Some philosophers want a foundation. Others accept a circle, a whole connected system, or an infinite series.
An explanation may answer why each item has a feature without answering why the whole series exists at all.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic teaches us not to reject an idea just because it sounds strange. We should find out exactly what the endless chain shows. It also helps us notice the difference between explaining each small part and explaining the entire system. These are useful habits whenever we study causes, reasons, rules, or evidence.

important_terms.definition: A series that starts with one item and keeps going, with a next item but no final item.
A reason for thinking that an idea or theory has a problem because it leads to an endless series.
A basic starting point that does not need to be supported by another item of the same kind.
The idea that some things can support one another as a group, rather than needing one first support.
The idea that an endless series may be acceptable and does not always show that a theory is mistaken.

questions_to_think_about: Does every explanation need a first explanation?
Can an endless list be useful even if it has no last item?
Is explaining each block enough, or must we explain why the whole tower stands?
Would you rather have one strong foundation or many connected supports?

summaries.example: Suppose every belief is justified only by another justified belief. Belief P is supported by reason R1, R1 by R2, and so on without end. A foundationalist says the chain must eventually reach a reason that needs no further justified reason. An infinitist accepts the endless chain. A coherentist instead says that justification belongs primarily to a mutually supporting system of beliefs. The disagreement concerns not merely whether the chain is infinite, but what justification requires.
summaries.summary: An infinite regress argument begins with a chain whose members are related in a suitable way and which has no final member. Such an argument may challenge a theory in different ways. The regress may expose a contradiction in the theory's principles, as in a version of the Third Man objection, or it may reveal a local problem, such as an infinite domain where independent evidence suggests the domain is finite. In other cases, the alleged defect is failure of explanation. Foundationalists stop the chain with basic items; coherentists appeal to a circular or holistic structure; infinitists accept the endless sequence. The entry emphasizes that these options cannot be assessed without asking what is being explained, whether the explanation is transmissive, and whether simplicity or unity favors one theory over another.
key_ideas: A regress can be objectionable because it produces a contradiction, a context-specific defect, or a failure to meet the theory's explanatory aim.
The fact that a theory generates infinitely many entities is not by itself a contradiction; whether it is a problem may depend on the subject matter.
A regress of natural numbers and a regress of causes can have the same structure while differing in acceptability because of independent reasons about numbers, events, or time.
The distinction between local and global explanation is central: each member may be explained even when the existence of the whole series is not.
Not every explanatory chain transmits the feature being explained. This leaves room for some infinitist responses to regress arguments.
Parsimony and unified explanation can provide reasons to prefer a foundational theory without proving that infinite regresses are impossible.
summaries.why_it_matters: Regress arguments test the standards used in philosophical explanation. They show that 'infinite' does not have one automatic philosophical meaning: an infinite sequence may be inconsistent, extravagant, harmless, or incomplete relative to a particular explanatory goal. The analysis also separates metaphysical dependence from other relations, such as giving reasons or comparing rates. This prevents a regress objection from proving more than its premises support.

important_terms.definition: An argument that uses an endless sequence to challenge a theory, either because the sequence reveals another defect or because the sequence itself is alleged to be unacceptable.
A defect in a theory that gives us reason to reject it. A global vice is generally bad; a local vice is bad given a particular subject or goal.
A theory or view holding that some items are fundamental and do not depend on further items of the relevant kind.
A view that explains at least some items through relations within a connected whole, rather than through a single foundational starting point.
The position that an infinite chain can be accepted rather than stopped by a foundation or replaced by a holistic account.
Dependence in which one thing exists or has its nature partly because of another thing.
An explanation of one item that relies on another item having the relevant feature, with that explanatory role continuing through the chain.
An explanation that refers to another item having a feature without making the other item's having that feature part of what explains the first.

questions_to_think_about: What independent evidence would make an infinite domain a local theoretical vice?
Is explaining every member of a series enough, or must a theory also explain why the series exists?
Can a coherent system provide justification without simply reasoning in a circle?
When does an additional entity make a theory less plausible, and when is it harmless?
Does an infinite regress show impossibility, or can it merely show that a theory has an explanatory cost?

summaries.example: Think about natural numbers. Zero has a successor, one; one has a successor, two; two has a successor, three; and the pattern continues forever. Most people do not see this as a bad regress. Now compare a rule saying that every event must have an earlier cause. If every cause is itself an event with an earlier cause, the rule creates an endless past chain. That might seem more troubling if we have independent reasons to think the past contains only finitely many events. The same pattern can therefore be acceptable in one case and questionable in another.
summaries.summary: An infinite regress is an endless sequence in which each member is related to the next. Philosophers use regress arguments to challenge theories, but the challenge can work in more than one way. A regress may reveal a contradiction, or it may reveal another defect that matters only in a particular context. For example, an infinite sequence of natural numbers is usually not considered a problem, while an infinite chain of earlier causes may conflict with what we think about the past. Regresses can also raise questions about explanation. If every item is explained by another item of the same kind, do we explain each item successfully, or does the whole series still lack an explanation? Philosophers answer with foundations, coherent systems, or acceptance of an infinite chain.
key_ideas: An infinite regress is not automatically vicious or mistaken.
A regress is easier to reject when it leads to a contradiction already known to be unacceptable.
The same structure can be fine for natural numbers but problematic for events if there are independent reasons to think there cannot be infinitely many such events.
A theory can explain why each individual item has a feature while failing to explain why the whole series has that feature at all.
Foundationalism, coherentism, and infinitism offer different responses to the demand for support or explanation.
Parsimony may count against an infinite theory even when the theory is not logically inconsistent or impossible.
summaries.why_it_matters: Regress arguments help us examine hidden assumptions in explanations. They make us ask whether a theory needs a first step, whether an endless chain really causes a contradiction, and whether explaining each part is different from explaining the whole. These questions appear in discussions of knowledge, existence, morality, time, and the structure of theories.

important_terms.definition: A chain that begins with one member but continues by adding related members forever, without reaching a last member.
A philosophical challenge claiming that an endless chain creates a problem for a theory.
A flaw in a theory. Some flaws are bad for nearly any theory, while others are bad only because of the theory's particular subject or goal.
The view that some basic facts or things stop the need for further support and can support other facts or things.
The view that support can come from a connected group or system, rather than from one first foundation.
The view that an endless chain can be a genuine option instead of something that must be stopped.
A relation in which one thing depends on another for its existence or for being the kind of thing it is.
An explanation in which the feature of a later item helps explain the same feature in an earlier item, so the explanatory role is passed along the chain.

questions_to_think_about: Why might an endless list of numbers seem less worrying than an endless list of past events?
Does a theory need to explain every fact, or only the facts it set out to explain?
How is a whole system of mutual support different from two claims that simply support each other in a circle?
Can a theory be possible but still less attractive because it adds too many entities?
